K.title: Pat-a-Cake
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake, baker's man. Bake me a cake as fast as you can. Pat it and prick it and mark it with B. Put it in the oven for baby and me.

K.title: Row, Row, Row Your Boat
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Row, row, row your boat gently down the stream. Merrily, merrily, merrily, merrily, life is but a dream.

K.title: Baa, Baa, Black Sheep
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool? Yes sir, yes sir, three bags full. One for my master, one for my dame, and one for the little boy who lives down the lane.

K.title: Little Bo Peep
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Little Bo Peep has lost her sheep and does not know where to find them. Leave them alone and they will come home, bringing their tails behind them.

K.title: Rain, Rain, Go Away
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Rain, rain, go away. Come again some other day. Little children want to play. Rain, rain, go away.

K.title: Star Light, Star Bright
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Star light, star bright, first star I see tonight. I wish I may, I wish I might, have the wish I wish tonight.

K.title: Bye Baby Bunting
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Bye baby bunting, daddy's gone a hunting. He'll bring home a rabbit skin to wrap the baby bunting in.

K.title: Hot Cross Buns
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Hot cross buns, hot cross buns. One a penny, two a penny, hot cross buns. If your daughters do not like them, give them to your sons.

K.title: Jack Be Nimble
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Jack be nimble, Jack be quick. Jack jump over the candlestick. He jumped high, he jumped low. Jack jumped over and away he did go.

K.title: Old MacDonald Had a Farm
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Old MacDonald had a farm, ee-i-ee-i-o. And on that farm he had a cow, ee-i-ee-i-o. With a moo moo here and a moo moo there, here a moo, there a moo, everywhere a moo moo.

K.title: The Itsy Bitsy Spider
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: The itsy bitsy spider climbed up the water spout. Down came the rain and washed the spider out. Out came the sun and dried up all the rain. And the itsy bitsy spider climbed up the spout again.

K.title: Polly Put the Kettle On
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Polly put the kettle on, we'll all have tea. Polly put the kettle on, Polly put the kettle on, we'll all have tea.

K.title: Mary Had a Little Lamb
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Mary had a little lamb, little lamb, little lamb. Mary had a little lamb, its fleece was white as snow.

K.title: Jack and Jill
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water. Jack fell down and broke his crown, and Jill came tumbling after.

K.title: Humpty Dumpty
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall. Humpty Dumpty had a great fall. All the king's horses and all the king's men could not put Humpty together again.

K.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
K.author: Aesop
K.passage: The Ant and the Grasshopper. In a field one summer's day a Grasshopper was hopping about, chirping and singing to its heart's content. An Ant passed by, bearing along with great toil an ear of corn he was taking to the nest.

K.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
K.author: Aesop
K.passage: The Tortoise and the Hare. A Hare one day ridiculed the short feet and slow pace of the Tortoise. The Tortoise laughed and said, I will race you. The Hare agreed, and off they went together.

K.title: Goldilocks and the Three Bears
K.author: Traditional
K.passage: Goldilocks and the Three Bears. Once upon a time there were Three Bears who lived in a little house in the woods. One day Goldilocks came to their house. She knocked on the door, but no one answered.

1.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit
1.author: Beatrix Potter
1.passage: Once upon a time there were four little rabbits whose names were Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter. They lived with their mother in a sand-bank underneath the root of a very big fir-tree.

1.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit (Mother's Warning)
1.author: Beatrix Potter
1.passage: Now, my dears, said old Mrs. Rabbit, you may go into the fields or down the lane, but don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden. Your Father had an accident there; he was put in Mrs. McGregor's pie by Mrs. McGregor.

1.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit (Peter's Adventure)
1.author: Beatrix Potter
1.passage: Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail, who were good little bunnies, went down the lane to gather blackberries. But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's garden and squeezed under the gate.

1.title: The Lion and the Mouse
1.author: Aesop
1.passage: The Lion and the Mouse. A mighty Lion was sleeping in the sun. A little Mouse, not seeing the Lion, ran across his paw and woke him up. The Lion grabbed the Mouse and was about to swallow him.

1.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
1.author: Aesop
1.passage: The Boy Who Cried Wolf. A shepherd boy tended his flock near a dark forest. One day he cried out, Wolf! Wolf! The villagers came running to help him, but there was no wolf.

1.title: The Ugly Duckling
1.author: Hans Christian Andersen
1.passage: The Ugly Duckling. It was beautiful summer weather in the country. The wheat was golden, the oats were still green, and the grass grew thick around the little pools. There sat a duck on her nest, watching her eggs.

1.title: The Land of Nod
1.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
1.passage: The Land of Nod. From breakfast on through all the day at home among my friends I stay. But every night I go away to the Land of Nod.

2.title: The Velveteen Rabbit (What is Real?)
2.author: Margery Williams
2.passage: What is real? asked the Rabbit one day. Does it mean having things that buzz inside you and a stick-out handle? Real isn't how you are made, said the Skin Horse. It's a thing that happens to you.

2.title: The Velveteen Rabbit (The Boy's Love)
2.author: Margery Williams
2.passage: The Boy loved the Velveteen Rabbit so hard that he loved all his hair off, and the pink came off the end of his nose where the Boy's cheek had rubbed against it. But the Rabbit didn't mind.

2.title: The Jungle Book (Night Verse)
2.author: Rudyard Kipling
2.passage: Now Chil the Kite brings home the night that Mang the Bat set free. The herds are shut in byre and hut for loosed till dawn are we. This is the hour of pride and power, talon and tush and claw.

2.title: How the Leopard Got His Spots
2.author: Rudyard Kipling
2.passage: How the Leopard Got His Spots. In the days when everybody started fair, Best Beloved, the Leopard lived in a place called the High Veldt.

2.title: The Emperor's New Clothes
2.author: Hans Christian Andersen
2.passage: The Emperor's New Clothes. There was once a vain Emperor who cared for nothing but his appearance. He spent all his money on fine clothes and wanted a new suit every day.

2.title: Cinderella
2.author: Traditional
2.passage: Cinderella. Once upon a time there lived a beautiful girl named Cinderella. She lived with her stepmother and two stepsisters who were very unkind to her and made her do all the work.

2.title: The Fox and the Grapes
2.author: Aesop
2.passage: The Fox and the Grapes. A hungry Fox saw some ripe grapes hanging high on a vine. He jumped again and again, trying to reach them, but they were too high.

3.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (Sitting by Sister)
3.author: Lewis Carroll
3.passage: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do. Once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it.

3.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (White Rabbit)
3.author: Lewis Carroll
3.passage: So she was considering in her own mind whether the pleasure of making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up and picking the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her.

3.title: The Jungle Book (Mowgli and Baloo)
3.author: Rudyard Kipling
3.passage: Mowgli was a boy who lived in the jungle with the wolves. Baloo the bear was teaching him the Law of the Jungle. All the jungle folk knew Mowgli and he knew them.

3.title: How the Whale Got His Throat
3.author: Rudyard Kipling
3.passage: How the Whale Got His Throat. In the sea, once upon a time, there was a Whale who ate all the fishes. The fishes were much displeased at this, and they held a meeting.

3.title: The Little Mermaid
3.author: Hans Christian Andersen
3.passage: The Little Mermaid. Far out in the deep sea where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, there lived the Sea King with his mermaid daughters.

3.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit (Meadow Warning)
3.author: Beatrix Potter
3.passage: Peter's mother said, You may go anywhere in the meadow or down the lane, but you must NOT go into Mr. McGregor's garden. The other rabbits obeyed, but Peter was always a naughty little rabbit.

3.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
3.author: Aesop
3.passage: The Crow and the Pitcher. A thirsty Crow found a pitcher with a little water at the bottom. He tried to drink from it, but his beak was too long and could not reach the water.

4.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (The Rabbit with Watch)
4.author: Lewis Carroll
4.passage: Down the Rabbit-Hole. I shall be late! thought Alice as she hurried along. But when the Rabbit actually took a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket, she thought: This is curious! What an odd thing a watch is!

4.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (Falling Down)
4.author: Lewis Carroll
4.passage: Alice fell down, down, down. The Rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel and then dipped suddenly down. She had not a moment to think about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very deep well.

4.title: The Jungle Book (Shere Khan and Mowgli)
4.author: Rudyard Kipling
4.passage: Shere Khan the Tiger was lame in one foot, and so he roamed the jungle slowly. All the creatures feared him. But Mowgli, the boy raised by wolves, did not know fear as other animals knew it.

4.title: Robinson Crusoe (Opening)
4.author: Daniel Defoe
4.passage: I was born in York, in a good family, though not of that country. My father being a merchant of great repute, he desired that I should learn a trade or go to sea.

4.title: How the Camel Got His Hump
4.author: Rudyard Kipling
4.passage: How the Camel Got His Hump. Now this is the next tale, and it tells how the Camel got his big hump. The Camel lived in the Howling Desert. The Horse came to him on Monday morning.

4.title: The Steadfast Tin Soldier
4.author: Hans Christian Andersen
4.passage: The Steadfast Tin Soldier. There were once five-and-twenty tin soldiers, all brothers, for they had been made out of the same old tin spoon. They were dressed in blue and red uniforms and stood straight with their guns.

4.title: The Three Little Pigs
4.author: Traditional
4.passage: The Three Little Pigs. Once upon a time there were three little pigs who lived with their mother. When they grew up, she said to them, The world is a big place. Go out and build houses of your own.

5+.title: A Tale of Two Cities (Opening)
5+.author: Charles Dickens
5+.passage: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to Heaven, we were all going direct the other way—in short, the period was so far like the present period, that some of its noisiest authorities insisted on its being received, for good or for evil, in the superlative degree of comparison only.

5+.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (A Scandal in Bohemia)
5+.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
5+.passage: To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer.

5+.title: The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (Opening)
5+.author: Mark Twain
5+.passage: You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mainly. There was things which he stretched, but mainly he told the truth. That is nothing. I never seen anybody but lied one time or another, without it was Aunt Polly, or the widow Douglas. It is the best way; the way it ought to be.

5+.title: The Twelve Dancing Princesses
5+.author: Brothers Grimm
5+.passage: In a certain kingdom there lived a king who had twelve daughters, each one more beautiful than the other. They slept together in a large hall, and every night the doors were locked and barred. But in the morning it was found that their shoes had been worn into holes during the night, as if they had been danced in. How this happened no one could explain, and the king became deeply troubled. He sent out a proclamation that whosoever could discover where the princesses danced during the night should have one of them for his wife.

Adult.title: A Tale of Two Cities (Extended Opening)
Adult.author: Charles Dickens
Adult.passage: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us, we were all going direct to Heaven, we were all going direct the other way—in short, the period was so far like the present period, that some of its noisiest authorities insisted on its being received, for good or for evil, in the superlative degree of comparison only. There were a king with a large jaw and a queen with a plain face, on the throne of England; there were a king with a large jaw and a queen with a fair face, on the throne of France.

Adult.title: Pride and Prejudice (Opening)
Adult.author: Jane Austen
Adult.passage: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters. My dear Mr. Bennet, said his lady to him one day, have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?

Adult.title: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Opening)
Adult.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
Adult.passage: Mr. Utterson the lawyer was a man of rugged countenance that was never lighted by a smile; cold, scanty and embarrassed in discourse; backward in sentiment; lean, long, dusty, dreary and yet somehow lovable. At friendly meetings, and when the wine was to his taste, something eminently human beaconed from his eye; something indeed which never found its way into his talk, but which spoke not only in these silent symbols of the after-dinner face, but more often and loudly in the acts of his life.
